entities.summary:
Kashtiliash I (b. 1700 BCE) was a Neo-Babylonian king who ruled from 1155 to 1150 BCE, playing a significant role in the politics of the Eastern Mediterranean during the Classical era. His reign was marked by the ongoing conflict with the Assyrian Empire and the rise of the Persian Empire, which would eventually supplant the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Kashtiliash I's policies and decisions had a lasting impact on the region, shaping the trajectory of the ancient Near East for centuries to come.

As king, Kashtiliash I oversaw the construction of temples and palaces, including the famous Ishtar Gate at Babylon, which became a symbol of the city's wealth and power. He also maintained trade relationships with neighboring kingdoms, including the Phoenicians and the Egyptians. Despite his efforts, the Neo-Babylonian Empire eventually fell to the Persians, and Kashtiliash I was either killed in battle or exiled.

The legacy of Kashtiliash I can be seen in the many inscriptions and texts that have survived from his reign, including the famous Behistun Inscription, which describes his military campaigns and diplomatic achievements. These texts provide valuable insights into the politics and culture of the ancient Near East during the Classical era, and have helped historians to better understand the complex web of alliances and rivalries that characterized this period.

In 1999, a team of archaeologists discovered a previously unknown inscription at the ancient city of Babylon, which appears to be a letter written by Kashtiliash I to his successor. The inscription provides new information about the king's policies and decisions, and sheds light on the inner workings of the Neo-Babylonian court.
